articles.title: New Colorado neighborhood could offer glimpse into the future of home energy use
articles.content:
A new residential development south of Denver is the testing ground for an unusual partnership that could transform home heating and cooling across the country.

Dandelion Energy, a geothermal startup, and Lennar, one of the nation’s largest homebuilders, recently completed construction of nearly 100 homes at the base of Colorado’s Front Range, each equipped with its own ground-source heat pump. The systems use less electricity than even the most efficient air-source heat pumps, potentially helping Colorado meet its climate goals while reducing peak energy demand and eliminating the need for new gas pipelines.

Ground-source heat pumps draw on steady temperatures belowground to help heat and cool buildings. However, the projects’ custom designs and drilling requirements—homes typically require one or more boreholes drilled several hundred feet deep—are pricey. Drilling alone often costs more than $10,000.

Dandelion, a company that got its start at X—a “moonshot” research and development subsidiary of Alphabet, Google’s parent company—says it can complete geothermal heating and cooling projects twice as fast and at half the cost of similar installations.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

Geothermal startup Dandelion Energy and homebuilder Lennar recently completed nearly 100 homes with geothermal heating and cooling at the Ken Caryl Ranch housing development in Littleton, Colorado. Phil McKenna / Inside Climate News

The company is “taking a kind of mass market and maximally efficient lens to what has historically been a bespoke kind of custom, high-end product,” said Dan Yates, Dandelion Energy’s CEO and chairman.

Earlier this year at Lennar’s Ken Caryl Ranch development, Dandelion’s drill team demonstrated a lightweight rig designed to quickly move from lot to lot, drilling boreholes and installing polyethylene pipe across the sprawling housing development before building foundations are poured.

Each home gets a single bore between 200 and 500 feet deep, where temperatures are approximately 50 degrees Fahrenheit year-round. Water circulating through the pipe is warmed or cooled by the surrounding earth before a heat pump installed in the basement of each new home provides additional heating or cooling depending on the time of year.

Dandelion’s drilling team can complete boreholes for one or more homes per day. If they had to drill a similar installation elsewhere for a single building, they could lose an entire day simply transporting the rig to and from the site.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

Geothermal startup Dandelion Energy and homebuilder Lennar recently completed nearly 100 homes with geothermal heating and cooling in Littleton. Phil McKenna / Inside Climate News

Installing the devices across dozens of similar new homes at once also eliminates the need for custom plans for each building and avoids potentially costly retrofits to the buildings’ heating, ventilation, and air conditioning systems.

The end result is a highly efficient heating and cooling system that Dandelion says outcompetes air-source heat pumps and conventional gas heating systems. This is especially true during cold snaps, when energy demand peaks and ground-source heat pumps use a quarter as much electricity as air-source heat pumps, Yates said.

It’s “the only system that actually reduces peak demand and electrifies homes at the same time,” he said.

The Ken Caryl Ranch development is part of a larger initiative the company launched with Lennar in 2025 to install geothermal heating and cooling at more than 1,500 homes in Colorado over two years. Dandelion hopes to scale up to 10,000 homes per year nationwide in the coming years.

“Our mission at Dandelion is to mainstream geothermal, and we think that the time has finally arrived for that to happen,” Yates said.

Just over a million U.S. homes have ground-source heat pumps, with approximately 100,000 new installations each year, according to a 2025 U.S. Department of Energy report. The agency found that geothermal heating and cooling could reach 7 million homes by 2035. Doing so would reduce winter peak energy demand by more than 40 gigawatts nationwide, resulting in roughly $4 billion in annual savings in U.S. electric grid costs, according to the report.

Ground-source heat pumps currently make up just a small fraction of new home heating and cooling systems. By contrast, 3.6 million air-source heat pumps were sold in the U.S. last year, outpacing gas furnace sales for the fourth year in a row, said Yara van Ingen, an associate with BloombergNEF’s building decarbonization team.

Ground-source heat pumps are economically viable across the continental United States, according to a study published this month in the journal iScience that considered incentives, energy costs and local climate and subsurface conditions.

“It is technically possible everywhere, and there is economic potential across all states,” said Juliet Simpson, a former research engineer at the National Laboratory of the Rockies and the study’s lead author.

A primary challenge for ground-source heat pumps is their upfront cost, which averages around $25,000 for a typical new home, according to the Energy Department report. Van Ingen added that space constraints, especially in dense urban environments, as well as permitting requirements that vary across the U.S. can also complicate borehole drilling.

Dandelion and Lennar, an investor in the geothermal company, are among those working to lower costs. But incentives and policy changes also help. An energy efficiency program by Xcel Energy, Colorado’s largest gas and electric utility company, provides approximately $25,000 per home for new, high-efficiency buildings with a ground-source heat pump to offset added building and heat pump costs.

“For large neighborhoods with hundreds of homes, builders may receive seven-figure rebate amounts,” an Xcel spokesperson said in a written statement.

Geothermal pipes run through the basement of each building. Phil McKenna / Inside Climate News

The rebates help Xcel advance its climate goals and meet Colorado’s Clean Heat Standard requirement to reduce greenhouse gas emissions 22 percent below 2015 levels by 2030.

Colorado also provides a $2,000 tax credit for ground-source heat pumps and requires homebuilders to pay for new gas service expansion pipes, costs that are not incurred if developers build all-electric homes.

Policies that incentivize high-efficiency electric heating and cooling while discouraging fossil fuel use in homes are intended to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from buildings, said Will Toor, executive director at the Colorado Energy Office.

Other states and utility companies also offer incentives for ground-source heat pumps, including Maryland, where Dandelion recently announced plans to install the technology in 129 new homes. In addition, commercial ground-source heat pump projects are now eligible for federal tax credits that cover 30 percent or more of total installation costs.

“The economics just look better and better,” Jessica Silber-Byrne, senior manager of thermal energy networks for the Building Decarbonization Coalition, a nonprofit organization working to eliminate the use of fossil fuels in buildings. “There is a combination of both incentives and market signals that suggest that this is about to really take off.”
articles.reasoning: The article describes a significant real-world advancement in home energy technology through the large-scale deployment of affordable geothermal heating and cooling systems in new residential developments. This innovation has broad potential to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, lower energy demand peaks, and help meet climate goals, benefiting many people and the environment. The article provides detailed context on the technology, partnerships, scale, and policy incentives, demonstrating substantial positive impact and feasibility for nationwide adoption.
articles.personality_title: Colorado neighborhood pioneers affordable geothermal heating for homes
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – A new housing area near Denver is testing a new way to heat and cool homes using the earth’s natural temperature. This method, called geothermal heating and cooling, could change how homes use energy across the U.S.

**What happened** – Two companies, Dandelion Energy and Lennar, built nearly 100 new homes in Colorado with ground-source heat pumps. These pumps use underground temperatures to heat or cool homes more efficiently than usual systems. The project used a new drilling technique that is faster and cheaper, making it easier to install these systems in many homes at once.

**Impact** – This method uses less electricity than regular heat pumps, especially in cold weather, which helps lower energy use when it is needed most. It also avoids the need for new gas pipelines, cutting greenhouse gas emissions. The project shows that geothermal heating can be affordable and practical for many homes, not just expensive custom buildings.

**What's next step** – The companies plan to install geothermal heating in over 1,500 homes in Colorado soon and aim to expand to 10,000 homes per year across the country. More states and utilities are offering money to help pay for these systems, making them easier for builders and homeowners to choose.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A new Colorado neighborhood is proving that affordable geothermal heating and cooling can help homes save energy and reduce pollution on a large scale.
articles.personality_title_fr: Un quartier du Colorado innove avec le chauffage géothermique abordable pour les maisons
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Un nouveau quartier résidentiel près de Denver teste une nouvelle façon de chauffer et refroidir les maisons en utilisant la température naturelle de la terre. Cette méthode, appelée chauffage et refroidissement géothermiques, pourrait changer la consommation d’énergie des maisons aux États-Unis.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Deux entreprises, Dandelion Energy et Lennar, ont construit près de 100 nouvelles maisons dans le Colorado équipées de pompes à chaleur géothermiques. Ces pompes utilisent la température du sol pour chauffer ou refroidir les maisons plus efficacement que les systèmes classiques. Le projet a utilisé une nouvelle technique de forage plus rapide et moins coûteuse, facilitant l’installation dans plusieurs maisons en même temps.

**Impact** – Cette méthode consomme moins d’électricité que les pompes à chaleur classiques, surtout en hiver, ce qui réduit la demande d’énergie aux moments critiques. Elle évite aussi la construction de nouveaux gazoducs, diminuant les émissions de gaz à effet de serre. Ce projet montre que le chauffage géothermique peut être abordable et pratique pour de nombreuses maisons, pas seulement pour des constructions coûteuses.

**Prochaines étapes** – Les entreprises prévoient d’installer ce chauffage géothermique dans plus de 1 500 maisons au Colorado bientôt et veulent étendre le projet à 10 000 maisons par an dans tout le pays. Plusieurs États et compagnies d’énergie offrent aussi des aides financières pour encourager ces installations.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Un nouveau quartier du Colorado démontre que le chauffage et refroidissement géothermiques abordables peuvent aider les maisons à économiser de l’énergie et réduire la pollution à grande échelle.
articles.personality_title_es: Nuevo barrio en Colorado apuesta por calefacción geotérmica asequible para hogares
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Un nuevo desarrollo residencial cerca de Denver está probando una nueva forma de calentar y enfriar casas usando la temperatura natural del suelo. Este método, llamado calefacción y refrigeración geotérmica, podría cambiar el uso de energía en hogares de todo Estados Unidos.

**Qué pasó** – Dos empresas, Dandelion Energy y Lennar, construyeron casi 100 casas nuevas en Colorado con bombas de calor de fuente terrestre. También evita la necesidad de nuevas tuberías de gas, reduciendo las emisiones de gases contaminantes. El proyecto demuestra que la calefacción geotérmica puede ser económica y práctica para muchas casas, no solo para construcciones caras.

**Próximo paso** – Las empresas planean instalar calefacción geotérmica en más de 1,500 casas en Colorado pronto y quieren expandirse a 10,000 casas por año en todo el país. Más estados y compañías eléctricas están ofreciendo incentivos para ayudar a pagar estos sistemas.

articles.title: Uganda’s UN-supported wildlife forensics lab turns ivory seizures into convictions
articles.summary: The package originated in Entebbe, Uganda, bound for Cairo, containing 10 kilograms of thumb-sized pieces that could have been either bone or elephant ivory.
articles.content:
When detectives from the Uganda Police Force and investigators from the Uganda Wildlife Authority intercepted the package in January 2025, they needed more than suspicion to investigate the person who sent the package.

The police sent a sample to the Uganda Wildlife Forensics and Timber Laboratory in Entebbe, a facility that has been supported since 2019 by the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC).

Scientists found a distinctive cross-hatched pattern associated with elephant ivory. DNA testing later confirmed that the material came from an elephant, lab manager Patrick Chiyo told UN News.

© European Union

Two months later, police arrested the man who sent the package. At his residence, investigators found additional elephant ivory, along with warthog ivory. He was charged with attempted trafficking and illegal possession and sentenced to 15 years in prison or a fine equivalent to 140 million Ugandan shillings – or more than $35,000 USD.

For Mr. Chiyo, the case illustrates why forensic evidence matters in the fight against wildlife crime: it can establish what an animal product is when traffickers have cut it into small pieces or removed the physical characteristics that would make it easy to identify.

“Poachers are removing identification features from wildlife carcasses to evade detection,” Mr. Chiyo said.

He added that DNA reports are increasingly being required by Uganda’s wildlife court and that suspects are pleading guilty more often thanks to the lab.

From seizure to science

Evidence from the UN’s 2024 World Wildlife Report shows that Uganda is as a significant hub of organised wildlife trafficking networks – especially of elephant ivory but also pangolin, a scaly anteater.

Tweet URL

In April, the Uganda Wildlife Forensics and Timber Laboratory opened with support from Denmark, the European Union and UNODC to help address the ivory issue.

It builds on a national training and technical support centre established in 2019 as a pilot wildlife forensics facility through a partnership involving UNODC, the TRACE Wildlife Forensics Network and the Ugandan Government. The earlier facility has assisted hundreds of investigations and prosecutions connected to illegal wildlife trade.

The lab’s work often begins far from Entebbe. Officers may seize sacks containing ivory pieces, pangolin scales or smoked bushmeat. Because these seizures can be bulky, scientists collect samples at police stations, documenting each step along the way.

Evidence is photographed before it is opened, and again after sampling. The original exhibit is returned to police custody, while sealed samples are transported to the lab for analysis.

The process can take a significant amount of time, Mr. Chiyo said, but it can be decisive, especially when animal remains are incomplete, altered or difficult to identify.

In one case in 2023, Mr. Chiyo travelled about four hours north of Kampala after a suspect was arrested with six skins, six heads, two sacks of meat, 24 hoofed legs and a fetus believed to be from wildlife. The skins appeared to come from antelope, but their exact identity could not be confirmed from appearance alone.

Mr. Chiyo and his team collected samples from the skins and fetus, then used DNA analysis to determine that they came from bushbucks. Mr. Chiyo later testified in court, and the suspect was sentenced to three years in prison.

Targeting wildlife crime

The lab most commonly receives evidence involving elephant ivory, bushmeat and pangolin scales, Mr. Chiyo said.

Bashir Hangi, from the Uganda Wildlife Authority, told UN News that elephants, pangolins, primates and some bird species are among the animals most threatened by illegal poaching and trade in Uganda.

Some people hunt animals for household consumption, while others kill wildlife for commercial gain, Mr. Chiyo said. Commercial trade is the larger threat for wildlife conservation, he added.

Although Mr. Chiyo said Uganda does not have a domestic market for ivory and pangolin scales, there is a thriving market for poached bushmeat. Authorities have encountered cases involving nearly a tonne of meat, he said.

Mr. Hangi said wildlife crime is driven both by organised criminal networks and by local communities facing economic hardship.

The impacts can also fall heavily on communities living near protected areas, where wildlife-related conflict and crop raiding have caused significant problems.

Mr. Chiyo said enforcement must reach the person who kills or captures an animal and those higher up in criminal networks who also profit. Prosecuting higher-ups requires more investment in interagency networks, he added.

© European Union

At the same time, he said, criminal justice is not enough. Alternative livelihoods are important, although they may not eliminate poaching linked to cultural values. He suggested a combined approach of livelihood support, preventive patrols and legal deterrence.

“A living wildlife is worth more benefits for many more people than a dead one,” Mr. Chiyo said.

New focus on timber

The Entebbe lab expanded into timber forensics in April, adding a new capability as Uganda confronts the environmental consequences of illegal logging and timber trafficking.

According to Ugandan authorities, Uganda’s forest cover has fallen from 24 per cent in 1990 to roughly 13 per cent in 2025, in large part due to timber trafficking. The new forensic capacity is intended to strengthen efforts to investigate illegal logging.

© Adobe/Pawel

Timber cases are more complicated than wildlife cases, Mr. Chiyo said, because harvesting is also permitted and regulated in many circumstances. Determining whether a piece of wood was obtained illegally can require additional steps and presents different challenges from identifying animal products.

The lab is only beginning to handle timber cases and has not yet seen evidence that illegal timber is moving through the same networks or routes as wildlife products, he said.

Critical for conservation

Still, the lab’s expansion reflects an increased recognition of the role of cracking down on wildlife and timber trafficking on protecting the environment.

Gladys Kamasanyu, the chief magistrate of the Uganda Wildlife Court, told UNODC in April that criminal justice and law enforcement can play a key role in these efforts.

“The forensic laboratory is critical to the criminal justice system, significantly enhancing the court’s ability to hold offenders accountable by providing objective, scientifically validated evidence to protect Uganda’s natural heritage for future generations,” Ms. Kamasanyu said.

Recognising the same relationship between law enforcement and conservation, Mr. Chiyo said his benchmark for success in the next few years would be “a sustainable and fully government supported wildlife and timber forensic laboratory in Uganda.”

At the current lab, however, each confirmed DNA sequence and seizure can help close the gap between a suspicion of trafficking and a prosecutable crime.

“Enhancing criminal justice through wildlife and timber forensics is an important pillar in environment protection,” Mr. Chiyo said. “Environmental justice will usually benefit the very vulnerable in society.”

articles.personality_title_fr: Le laboratoire de criminalistique animale de l’Ouganda transforme les saisies d’ivoire en condamnations
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – L’Ouganda fait face à de graves problèmes de commerce illégal d’animaux sauvages, notamment l’ivoire d’éléphant et les écailles de pangolin. Pour lutter contre cela, le pays a ouvert un laboratoire de criminalistique animale à Entebbe, soutenu par les Nations Unies et d’autres partenaires, pour utiliser la science dans les enquêtes sur la faune.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – En janvier 2025, la police ougandaise a intercepté un colis d’Entebbe à destination du Caire contenant de petits morceaux ressemblant à de l’ivoire. Ils ont envoyé des échantillons au laboratoire de criminalistique, où les scientifiques ont confirmé que le matériau était de l’ivoire d’éléphant grâce à des motifs spéciaux et des tests ADN. **Impact** – Cette affaire montre comment la science peut prouver ce que sont vraiment les produits animaux, même lorsque les trafiquants essaient de les cacher en les coupant ou en les modifiant. **Résumé en une phrase** – Le laboratoire de criminalistique animale soutenu par l’ONU en Ouganda transforme les preuves scientifiques en véritables condamnations contre le trafic illégal d’ivoire et de bois, renforçant les efforts de conservation.
articles.personality_title_es: El laboratorio forense de vida silvestre de Uganda convierte incautaciones de marfil en condenas
articles.personality_presentation_es:

Para combatir esto, el país abrió un laboratorio forense de vida silvestre en Entebbe, apoyado por las Naciones Unidas y otros socios, para usar la ciencia en investigaciones de crímenes contra la fauna.

articles.title: Woodlands project records more trees than expected
articles.summary: The Lost Woods of the Low Weald and Downs project aims to restore some of Sussex's ancient woodland.
articles.content:
A project which aims to restore ancient woodlands in Sussex has hit a significant "milestone" with over 5,500 trees now recorded.

Since March 2024, volunteers with the Lost Woods project have been recording ancient, veteran and notable trees across a 121-sq-miles (314-sq-km) area from Lewes to Storrington.

According to the latest figures, they have now recorded 5,570 trees, a number which Lost Woods outreach adviser, Bob Epsom, said is more than "we expected" and signifies a "milestone" for the project.

"When we look at the map of it, we can see the new clusters of trees being added...that's where the volunteers have been active," he said.

The Lost Woods is a partnership with four charities: Woodland Trust, Action in Rural Sussex, Sussex Wildlife Trust and Small Woods Association.

The work, funded by the National Lottery Heritage Fund, is part of a wider Lost Woods restoration programme which Epsom said comprises "19 individual projects".

About 20 volunteers are each given a square kilometre area to cover, and once recorded and verified, trees are added to the Ancient Tree Inventory which has been mapping the oldest and most important trees in the UK for 20 years.

The volunteers are working to find and record every ancient and veteran tree in the project area by next year, and Epsom, who leads the team, said they still "have a reasonable amount to cover".
articles.reasoning: The article describes a successful environmental conservation project restoring ancient woodlands in Sussex, involving community volunteers and multiple charities, with measurable progress and broad ecological significance.
articles.personality_title: Lost Woods project records over 5,500 ancient trees in Sussex
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The Lost Woods of the Low Weald and Downs project is working to restore ancient woodlands in Sussex, an area in southern England. Ancient and veteran trees are important because they support wildlife and help keep forests healthy.

**What happened** – Since March 2024, volunteers have been mapping and recording old and special trees across a large area from Lewes to Storrington. So far, they have found and recorded 5,570 trees, which is more than expected. The volunteers each cover a section of land and add the trees they find to the Ancient Tree Inventory, a list that tracks the oldest trees in the UK.

**Impact** – This milestone shows the project is making good progress in protecting and restoring ancient woodlands. The work helps preserve important natural habitats and raises awareness about the value of old trees. It also brings together four charities and community volunteers, showing how people can work together for the environment.

**What's next step** – Volunteers will continue to search for and record more ancient and veteran trees in the area until next year. The data collected will help guide future conservation efforts and ensure these woodlands are cared for in the long term.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The Lost Woods project has successfully mapped thousands of ancient trees in Sussex, marking an important step in protecting and restoring the region’s historic woodlands.
articles.personality_title_fr: Le projet Lost Woods recense plus de 5 500 arbres anciens dans le Sussex
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Le projet Lost Woods of the Low Weald and Downs vise à restaurer les anciennes forêts du Sussex, dans le sud de l’Angleterre. Les arbres anciens et vétérans sont importants car ils soutiennent la faune et maintiennent la santé des forêts.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Depuis mars 2024, des bénévoles cartographient et recensent les arbres vieux et remarquables sur une grande zone allant de Lewes à Storrington. Jusqu’à présent, ils ont trouvé et enregistré 5 570 arbres, un nombre supérieur aux attentes. Chaque bénévole couvre une zone et ajoute les arbres trouvés à l’Inventaire des Arbres Anciens, une liste des plus vieux arbres du Royaume-Uni.

**Impact** – Ce jalon montre que le projet progresse bien dans la protection et la restauration des anciennes forêts. Ce travail aide à préserver des habitats naturels importants et sensibilise à la valeur des vieux arbres. Il réunit aussi quatre associations et des bénévoles, montrant comment les gens peuvent agir ensemble pour l’environnement.

**Prochaine étape** – Les bénévoles continueront à chercher et enregistrer d’autres arbres anciens et vétérans dans la région jusqu’à l’année prochaine. Les données recueillies aideront à orienter les futures actions de conservation pour protéger ces forêts sur le long terme.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Le projet Lost Woods a cartographié avec succès des milliers d’arbres anciens dans le Sussex, marquant une étape importante pour la protection et la restauration des forêts historiques de la région.
articles.personality_title_es: El proyecto Lost Woods registra más de 5.500 árboles antiguos en Sussex
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – El proyecto Lost Woods of the Low Weald and Downs trabaja para restaurar bosques antiguos en Sussex, una zona del sur de Inglaterra. Los árboles antiguos y veteranos son importantes porque apoyan a la vida silvestre y mantienen los bosques saludables.

**Qué pasó** – Desde marzo de 2024, voluntarios han estado mapeando y registrando árboles viejos y especiales en una gran área que va de Lewes a Storrington. Hasta ahora, han encontrado y registrado 5.570 árboles, una cifra mayor a la esperada. Cada voluntario cubre una zona y añade los árboles encontrados al Inventario de Árboles Antiguos, una lista que registra los árboles más viejos del Reino Unido.

**Impacto** – Este logro muestra que el proyecto avanza bien en la protección y restauración de los bosques antiguos. El trabajo ayuda a preservar hábitats naturales importantes y aumenta la conciencia sobre el valor de los árboles viejos. También une a cuatro organizaciones benéficas y voluntarios, demostrando cómo las personas pueden trabajar juntas por el medio ambiente.

**Próximo paso** – Los voluntarios seguirán buscando y registrando más árboles antiguos y veteranos en la zona hasta el próximo año. Los datos recopilados ayudarán a guiar futuras acciones de conservación para cuidar estos bosques a largo plazo.

**Conclusión en una frase** – El proyecto Lost Woods ha logrado mapear miles de árboles antiguos en Sussex, marcando un paso importante en la protección y restauración de los bosques históricos de la región.

articles.title: I'm a wildlife cameraman but 'special' rare sightings can still take me by surprise
articles.summary: Wildlife cameraman Dan Abbot is caught off guard by a humpback whale, a rare sight in Welsh waters.
articles.content:
A wildlife cinematographer and shark guide has spoken about the unexpected surprise and joy of seeing a humpback whale in the Celtic Deep just off the Welsh coast.

Dan Abbot, known as Sharkman Dan on his social media, shared a recording of the exciting moment just off the Pembrokeshire coast.

He has seen the large marine mammals before, on planned trips where humpback whale sightings are not as unusual, but this experience was "a complete surprise".

Lloyd Nelmes from Sea Trust said the sighting was "unusual for someone who works in the field... who probably has their eyes on the water every day", adding, "for a normal person, it's insanely rare".
articles.reasoning: The article highlights a rare and positive wildlife sighting of a humpback whale in Welsh waters, suggesting potential positive environmental or conservation implications and inspiring public interest in marine life.

**What happened** – While filming near Pembrokeshire, Wales, Dan unexpectedly spotted a humpback whale in the Celtic Deep. Although he has seen these whales before on special trips, this sighting was a surprise because it happened without planning.

**Impact** – This sighting is unusual even for people like Dan who watch the sea closely every day. For most people, seeing a humpback whale in Welsh waters is extremely rare. It shows that these big whales might be visiting areas where they are not often noticed.

**What's next step** – The sighting could encourage more monitoring of whales in the area to learn why they are coming and how to protect them. It may also inspire people to take more interest in marine life and conservation efforts in Wales.
